doc.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: First direct confrontation with segregation at Howard Johnson's
summary: The band is told Negroes must eat around back in Washington, D.C., Carter's first in-your-face experience of the issue.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, it was eye-opening. One of the stops we made was in Washington, D.C. and we pulled up at Howard Johnsons and everyone got prepared to leave the bus and the bus driver went in first and came back and told us that they weren't serving Negroes in the front of the hotel, that we had to go around to the back. So that was my … my first large confrontation with that issue. The others were always one-one-one or rumor or innuendo, feeling that there's something wrong here. But that was my first in-your-face situation with that issue. Everybody grumbled and they did what they did and we ate our sandwiches and got out of town. That's what it is.
Among the lessons you were gathering was what I need to do for me, Ron, to make this work for me?

Well … probably on a less personal level but that's part of the issue … always survival, you know. Today … same … some kind of survival mechanisms in place and you figure out how to deal with it and get on with your life.
